title: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
section: 7.4 Inference of the Variance with Known Mean
text:
7.4 Inference of the Variance with Known Mean
Now assume \(\mu\) is known and infer \(\sigma^2\). Setting \(\nu = \sum_i (x_i - \mu)^2\), the likelihood is \[p(D \mid \mu, \sigma^2) \propto (\sigma^2)^{-n/2} \exp\left( -\frac{\nu}{2\sigma^2} \right).\]

Jeffreys prior for a scale parameter. Variance is a scale parameter: if we rescale \(x \to ax\), then \(\sigma^2 \to a^2\sigma^2\). As shown in Chapter 5 (§ Fisher information, Cramér–Rao, and the Jeffreys prior), the Jeffreys prior \(p_J(\theta) \propto \sqrt{\det \mathcal{I}(\theta)}\) is reparametrization-invariant. For the Gaussian scale parameter \(\sigma^2\) with known mean, the Fisher information is \(\mathcal{I}(\sigma^2) = n/[2(\sigma^2)^2]\), yielding \(p_J(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2\) (or equivalently \(p_J(\log\sigma^2) \propto 1\), uniform on log-scale). This prior ensures invariance under rescaling — critical for Bayes factors. Chapter 5 gives the extended example and invariance proof; here we apply it directly.
Inverse-Gamma conjugate family. The Inverse-Gamma distribution is conjugate for variance estimation.


If \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)\) with pdf \(f(x) = \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha-1} e^{-\beta x}\), then \(1/X \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)\) with pdf \[f(z) = \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} (1/z)^{\alpha+1} \exp(-\beta/z).\]

A prior \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}(\alpha_0, \beta_0)\) combined with the likelihood yields the conjugate posterior.

Inverse-Gamma Conjugate Update: \[\sigma^2 \mid D, \mu \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}\left( \alpha_0 + \frac{n}{2}, \beta_0 + \frac{\nu}{2} \right),\] where \(\nu = \sum_i (x_i - \mu)^2\).

The Jeffreys prior corresponds to \(\alpha_0 = 0\) and \(\beta_0 = 0\) (or \(\alpha_0 = -1/2\) to ensure integrability). The posterior mean is \(\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2 \mid D] = \beta_n/(\alpha_n - 1)\) for \(\alpha_n > 1\).

title: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
text:
7.5 Joint Inference: Normal-Inverse-Gamma Model
The most realistic case has both \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) unknown. Use a factorized prior \[p(\mu, \sigma^2) = p(\mu \mid \sigma^2) p(\sigma^2),\] with \(\mu \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \sigma^2/\kappa_0)\) and \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}(\alpha_0, \beta_0)\). This is the Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) conjugate family with hyperparameters \((\mu_0, \kappa_0, \alpha_0, \beta_0)\).

Posterior update. Combining likelihood with the NIG prior yields a posterior of the same form, with updated hyperparameters.


Normal-Inverse-Gamma Conjugate Update: \[\begin{align}
\kappa_n &= \kappa_0 + n, \\
\mu_n &= \frac{\kappa_0 \mu_0 + n\bar{x}}{\kappa_n}, \\
\alpha_n &= \alpha_0 + \frac{n}{2}, \\
\beta_n &= \beta_0 + \frac{S}{2} + \frac{\kappa_0 n}{2(\kappa_0 + n)} (\bar{x} - \mu_0)^2,
\end{align}\] where \(S = \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2\).

The joint posterior factorizes as \[p(\mu, \sigma^2 \mid D) \propto (\sigma^2)^{-(\alpha_n + 1)} \exp\left( -\frac{\beta_n}{\sigma^2} - \frac{\kappa_n(\mu - \mu_n)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right).\]

Marginal posterior of the mean. Marginalizing \(\sigma^2\) yields a Student-\(t\) posterior for \(\mu\).


The posterior marginal distribution of \(\mu\) given \(D\) is \[\mu \mid D \sim t_{2\alpha_n}\left( \mu_n, \frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n \kappa_n} \right),\] a Student-\(t\) distribution with \(\nu = 2\alpha_n\) degrees of freedom, location \(\mu_n\), and scale parameter \(\sqrt{\beta_n/(\alpha_n \kappa_n)}\).

Interpretation: the heavy tails of the \(t\)-distribution reflect additional uncertainty from not knowing \(\sigma^2\). For large \(n\), \(\nu = 2\alpha_n \approx n \to \infty\), so the \(t\)-distribution converges to a Gaussian, recovering asymptotic normality.

title: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
text:
7.6 Credible Intervals and Regions

Central credible interval for the mean. A central \((1-\alpha)\)% credible interval is \[\mu_n \pm t_{2\alpha_n, 1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n \kappa_n}},\] where \(t_{\nu, p}\) denotes the \(p\)-quantile of a Student-\(t\) distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom. Frequentist analogue: in the large-sample limit, this recovers the familiar confidence interval \(\hat{\mu} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2/n}\).
Joint credible region. A joint \((1-\alpha)\)% credible region for \(\theta = (\mu, \sigma^2)\) is the ellipse \[(\theta - \hat{\theta})^T \mathcal{I}_n(\hat{\theta}) (\theta - \hat{\theta}) \le \chi^2_{2, 1-\alpha},\] where \(\mathcal{I}_n(\hat{\theta})\) is the Fisher information matrix evaluated at the MLE and \(\chi^2_{2, 1-\alpha}\) is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of the chi-squared distribution with 2 degrees of freedom.

The posterior asymptotically factorizes: the estimated correlation between \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) vanishes as \(n \to \infty\). This convergence to Gaussian form and factorization is guaranteed by the Bernstein–von Mises theorem (Chapter 5, § Fisher information, Cramér–Rao, and the Jeffreys prior), which states that the posterior becomes approximately \(\mathcal{N}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{ML}}, \mathcal{I}_n(\theta_*)^{-1})\) for large \(n\), independently of the prior. This is why Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals asymptotically agree.

title: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
text:
7.7 Bayesian Hypothesis Testing

One-sided test for the mean. Consider \(H_0: \mu \le \mu^*\) vs \(H_1: \mu > \mu^*\). The posterior probability of \(H_1\) is \[P(H_1 \mid D) = 1 - F_t\left( \frac{\mu^* - \mu_n}{\sqrt{\beta_n/(\alpha_n \kappa_n)}} \right),\] where \(F_t\) is the CDF of a Student-\(t\) distribution with \(2\alpha_n\) degrees of freedom. Decision rule: reject \(H_0\) if \(P(H_1 \mid D) > 1 - \alpha\). Equivalently, reject if \(\mu^*\) lies below the lower bound of the \((1-\alpha)\)% credible interval.
Two-sided test and Bayes factor. For \(H_0: \mu = \mu^*\) vs \(H_1: \mu \ne \mu^*\), compare the marginal likelihoods.


The Bayes factor of \(H_1\) over \(H_0\) is \[\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(D \mid H_1)}{p(D \mid H_0)} = \frac{\int p(D \mid \mu, \sigma^2) p(\mu, \sigma^2 \mid H_1) d\mu d\sigma^2}{\int_{\mu=\mu^*} p(D \mid \mu^*, \sigma^2) p(\sigma^2 \mid H_0) d\sigma^2}.\]

Interpretation: \(\text{BF}_{10} > 1\) favors \(H_1\) (mean differs from \(\mu^*\)); \(\text{BF}_{10} < 1\) favors \(H_0\); the magnitude quantifies the strength of evidence. Unlike frequentist \(p\)-values, the Bayes factor is invariant under the choice of scale (the Jeffreys prior ensures this).

Bayesian \(t\)-test. The Bayesian \(t\)-test compares the observed \(t = (\bar{x} - \mu^*) / \sqrt{S/(n(n-1))}\) to its posterior predictive distribution under \(H_0\). With the NIG conjugate prior, the marginal likelihood under \(H_0\) is a \(t\)-distribution, naturally accounting for variance uncertainty without ad-hoc degrees-of-freedom corrections.
crumbs: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian

title: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
text:
7.8 Posterior Predictive Distribution
Given posterior \(p(\mu, \sigma^2 \mid D)\), the posterior predictive distribution for a new observation \(\tilde{x}\) is \[p(\tilde{x} \mid D) = \int p(\tilde{x} \mid \mu, \sigma^2) p(\mu, \sigma^2 \mid D) d\mu d\sigma^2.\]
For the NIG model, this marginalizes to a Student-\(t\) distribution with the same degrees of freedom and location as the posterior for \(\mu\), but with inflated scale (reflecting both parameter and observational uncertainty): \[\tilde{x} \mid D \sim t_{2\alpha_n}\left( \mu_n, \frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n} \left(1 + \frac{1}{\kappa_n}\right) \right).\]
The posterior predictive intervals are wider than credible intervals for the mean, appropriately quantifying full predictive uncertainty.
crumbs: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian

title: 7  Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
text:
7.9 Frequentist Contrast
The frequentist approach uses the sample \(t\)-statistic \[t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sqrt{S / (n(n-1))}},\] which under \(H_0: \mu = \mu^*\) follows \(t_{n-1}\). Rejection is based on \(p\)-value: \(p = P(|T| \ge |t_{\text{obs}}| \mid H_0)\).
Key differences from Bayes:

Frequentist \(t\)-test: assumes \(\mu^*\) exactly true under \(H_0\); \(p\)-value is the probability of observing data as extreme or more extreme under repeated sampling.
Bayesian \(t\)-test: posterior probability that \(\mu > \mu^*\) (or any specified region); updates beliefs given observed data; allows flexible loss functions for decision-making.
Sample size: Frequentist \(p\)-values can remain small for minor effects with large \(n\). Bayes factors adapt: as data accumulate under \(H_1\), they grow; but if data weakly support \(H_1\) relative to prediction, BF remains modest.
Asymptotic equivalence: For fixed effect size and large \(n\), frequentist confidence intervals and Bayesian credible intervals converge; the posterior becomes approximately Gaussian by Bernstein–von Mises.

text:
7.10 Illustrative Examples


Show code
set.seed(42)

mu_true <- 0.5
sigma_true <- 1.0

mu0 <- 0
sigma0 <- 2
n_list <- c(2, 20, 100)

mu_grid <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 2000)

par(mar = c(4.4, 4.4, 2.2, 1.2))
plot(NA, xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(0, 2.5), xlab = expression(mu), ylab = "Density", main = "")

for (i in seq_along(n_list)) {
  n <- n_list[i]
  x <- rnorm(n, mu_true, sigma_true)
  xbar <- mean(x)

  kappa_n <- 1/sigma0^2 + n/sigma_true^2
  mu_n <- (mu0/sigma0^2 + n*xbar/sigma_true^2) / kappa_n
  sigma_n <- sqrt(1/kappa_n)

  posterior_density <- dnorm(mu_grid, mu_n, sigma_n)
  col_vec <- c("black", "gray40", "#b8123e")
  lines(mu_grid, posterior_density, lwd = 1, lty = i, col = col_vec[i])
}

prior_density <- dnorm(mu_grid, mu0, sigma0)
lines(mu_grid, prior_density, lwd = 1, lty = 4, col = "gray70")

legend("topright", legend = c("Prior", "n=2", "n=20", "n=100"),
       lty = c(4, 1, 2, 3), col = c("gray70", "black", "gray40", "#b8123e"),
       lwd = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)





Posterior distribution for the mean under Normal-Normal conjugate model with known variance. As sample size increases (n=2, n=20, n=100), the posterior concentrates around the MLE and becomes narrower.






Show code
set.seed(123)

n <- 50
mu_true <- 0
sigma_true <- 1

x <- rnorm(n, mu_true, sigma_true)
xbar <- mean(x)
S <- sum((x - xbar)^2)

mu_hat <- xbar
sigma2_hat <- S / n

theta_hat <- c(mu_hat, sigma2_hat)

Sigma <- matrix(c(sigma2_hat / n, 0, 0, 2 * sigma2_hat^2 / n), 2, 2)

alpha_level <- 0.05
chi2_val <- qchisq(1 - alpha_level, df = 2)

eig <- eigen(Sigma)
A <- eig$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(eig$values * chi2_val))

angles <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 200)
circle <- rbind(cos(angles), sin(angles))
ellipse_mat <- A %*% circle
ellipse_df <- data.frame(
  mu = ellipse_mat[1,] + theta_hat[1],
  sigma2 = ellipse_mat[2,] + theta_hat[2]
)

par(mar = c(4.4, 4.4, 2.2, 1.2))
plot(ellipse_df$mu, ellipse_df$sigma2, type = "l", lwd = 1,
     xlab = expression(mu), ylab = expression(sigma^2),
     main = paste("n =", n),
     xlim = c(theta_hat[1] - 0.4, theta_hat[1] + 0.4),
     ylim = c(max(0, theta_hat[2] - 0.5), theta_hat[2] + 0.5))

points(theta_hat[1], theta_hat[2], pch = 19, col = "#b8123e", cex = 1)

legend("topright", legend = c("95% credible ellipse", "MLE"),
       lty = c(1, NA), pch = c(NA, 19), col = c("black", "#b8123e"),
       lwd = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)





95% credible region (ellipse) for the mean and variance. Shows asymptotic factorization: mean and variance are nearly uncorrelated in the large-sample limit.






Show code
mu_star <- 0
alpha0 <- 1.1
beta0 <- 0.5
kappa0 <- 0.01
mu0 <- 0

n <- 30
sigma_true <- 1

xbar_grid <- seq(-1, 2, length.out = 100)

log10_bf <- numeric(length(xbar_grid))

for (j in seq_along(xbar_grid)) {
  xbar <- xbar_grid[j]

  kappa_n <- kappa0 + n
  mu_n <- (kappa0*mu0 + n*xbar) / kappa_n
  alpha_n <- alpha0 + n/2

  S_approx <- 0
  beta_n <- beta0 + S_approx/2 + (kappa0*n)/(2*(kappa0+n)) * (xbar - mu0)^2

  log_bf <- 0.5*log(kappa0) - 0.5*log(kappa_n) +
            alpha0*log(beta0) - alpha_n*log(beta_n) +
            lgamma(alpha_n) - lgamma(alpha0) -
            0.5*log(pi) + 0.5*log(2*alpha_n) +
            lgamma(alpha_n - 0.5) - lgamma(alpha0 - 0.5)

  log10_bf[j] <- log_bf / log(10)
}

par(mar = c(4.4, 4.4, 2.2, 1.2))
plot(xbar_grid, log10_bf, type = "l", lwd = 1,
     xlab = expression(bar(x)), ylab = expression(log[10]*" BF"[1*","*0]),
     main = paste("Test: mu > 0, n =", n), col = "black")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray70", lwd = 1)
abline(v = mu_star, lty = 2, col = "gray40", lwd = 1)

legend("bottomright", legend = c("BF > 1: favor H_1", "BF = 1: indifferent", "BF < 1: favor H_0"),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.75)





Bayes factor BF_{1,0} (base 10 log scale) versus observed mean, for test H_0: mu <= 0 vs H_1: mu > 0. Shows transition from evidence favoring H_0 to H_1 as sample mean increases.

text:
7.11 Exercises

Conjugate Normal–Normal model with known variance. Observe \(n = 4\) measurements with sample mean \(\bar x = 2\) from \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2 = 1)\), with prior \(\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). Compute the posterior mean and variance.


Solution. Setup. We have \(n=4\) Gaussian observations with \(\bar x = 2\), known variance \(\sigma^2 = 1\), and a conjugate prior \(\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2) = \mathcal{N}(0,1)\); we want the posterior of \(\mu\). By the Normal–Normal conjugate update (§ Inference of the Mean with Known Variance), the posterior is Gaussian with precision equal to the sum of the prior precision and the data precision. Recall the derivation: multiplying the likelihood \(\propto \exp(-n(\bar x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2))\) by the prior \(\propto\exp(-(\mu-\mu_0)^2/(2\sigma_0^2))\) and completing the square in \(\mu\) isolates the coefficient of \(\mu^2\), which is \(\kappa_n/2\). Substituting the numbers, \[\kappa_n = \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2} = 1 + \frac{4}{1} = 5,\qquad V_n = \kappa_n^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{5}.\] The coefficient of the linear term in \(\mu\) inside the completed square yields the precision-weighted mean \[\mu_n = V_n\!\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n\bar x}{\sigma^2}\right) = \tfrac{1}{5}\bigl(0 + 4\cdot 2\bigr) = \tfrac{8}{5} = 1.6.\] Therefore \(\mu \mid D \sim \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\tfrac{8}{5},\ \tfrac{1}{5}\bigr)\). The MLE would be \(\bar x = 2\); the posterior mean is pulled toward \(\mu_0 = 0\) because the prior and data precisions are of comparable size (\(1\) vs \(4\)), so the prior still carries \(20\%\) weight.
Cross-reference: § Inference of the Mean with Known Variance (Normal–Normal conjugate update definition, and the worked example with \(n=9\), \(\sigma^2=4\), \(\bar x=3\)).


Same model as above. As \(n \to \infty\) with \(\bar x \to \mu_*\) fixed, what does the posterior tend to? State the result in terms of \(\mu_*\) and \(\sigma^2\).


Solution. Setup. With the same Normal–Normal conjugate model as above (\(\sigma^2 = 1\), prior \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)), we ask what happens to the posterior when the sample size grows without bound and \(\bar x \to \mu_*\). By the Normal–Normal conjugate update (§ Inference of the Mean with Known Variance), the posterior precision is \(\kappa_n = 1/\sigma_0^2 + n/\sigma^2\) and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average \(\mu_n = (\mu_0/\sigma_0^2 + n\bar x/\sigma^2)/\kappa_n\). As \(n \to \infty\), the data precision \(n/\sigma^2\) dominates the fixed prior precision \(1/\sigma_0^2\), so \[\kappa_n = \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2} = \frac{n}{\sigma^2}\!\left(1 + \frac{\sigma^2}{n\sigma_0^2}\right) \longrightarrow \frac{n}{\sigma^2}.\] Simultaneously the weight of the prior mean in \(\mu_n\) shrinks like \(1/n\): \(\mu_n = \bar x + O(1/n) \to \mu_*\). The posterior variance is \(V_n = 1/\kappa_n \to \sigma^2/n \to 0\). Therefore \[\mu \mid D \ \xrightarrow{n\to\infty}\ \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_*,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),\] which collapses to a point mass at \(\mu_*\) and coincides with the flat-prior posterior derived at the top of § Inference of the Mean with Known Variance. This is a concrete instance of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem cited at the end of § Credible Intervals and Regions: the influence of any proper prior with \(\sigma_0^2 < \infty\) vanishes in the large-sample limit, and Bayesian credible intervals coincide with frequentist confidence intervals.
Cross-reference: § Inference of the Mean with Known Variance (flat vs. conjugate prior); § Credible Intervals and Regions (Bernstein–von Mises).


Inference of the variance with known mean. Observe \(n\) i.i.d. samples from \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) with sum of squares \(S = \sum_i x_i^2\). Use the conjugate Inverse-Gamma prior \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \beta_0)\) and derive the posterior.


Solution. Setup. With \(n\) i.i.d. observations from \(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\) (known mean \(\mu=0\)) and an Inverse-Gamma prior \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0,\beta_0)\), we derive the posterior for the variance. By the Inverse-Gamma conjugacy for the variance (§ Inference of the Variance with Known Mean), with \(\mu=0\) the sufficient statistic \(\nu = \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\) collapses to \(S = \sum_i x_i^2\). The Gaussian likelihood as a function of \(\sigma^2\) alone is \[p(D\mid\sigma^2) \propto (\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{S}{2\sigma^2}\right),\] which has the kernel of an IG in \(\sigma^2\) with shape \(n/2-1\) and rate \(S/2\). The IG prior density is (by the definition in § Inference of the Variance with Known Mean) \[p(\sigma^2) \propto (\sigma^2)^{-(\alpha_0+1)}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta_0}{\sigma^2}\right).\] Multiplying likelihood and prior, the exponents in \((\sigma^2)^{-1}\) add and the terms in the exponential add: \[p(\sigma^2\mid D)\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(\alpha_0 + n/2 + 1)}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta_0 + S/2}{\sigma^2}\right).\] This is again the kernel of an Inverse-Gamma, so the posterior is \[\boxed{\ \sigma^2\mid D \sim \text{IG}\!\left(\alpha_n = \alpha_0 + \tfrac{n}{2},\ \beta_n = \beta_0 + \tfrac{S}{2}\right).\ }\] The shape is raised by \(n/2\) (each observation adds half a degree of freedom) and the rate is raised by half the observed sum of squares — conjugacy in its cleanest form. The posterior mean \(\beta_n/(\alpha_n-1)\) (valid for \(\alpha_n > 1\)) is a weighted average of prior mean and \(S/n\).
Cross-reference: § Inference of the Variance with Known Mean (Inverse-Gamma conjugate update theorem and IG definition).


Show that \((\bar x,\,s^2) = (\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i,\ \tfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2)\) are sufficient statistics for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\) in the i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) model, using the factorisation theorem.


Solution. Setup. We want to show that \((\bar x, s^2)\) carry all the information in \(D=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) about \((\mu,\sigma^2)\) when the data are i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). By the sufficiency definition in § Gaussian Sampling Model and Sufficient Statistics, a statistic \(T(D)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) iff the joint density factorises as \(p(D\mid\theta) = g(T(D);\theta)\cdot h(D)\) with \(h\) free of \(\theta\) (Fisher–Neyman theorem). The Gaussian joint density is \[p(D\mid\mu,\sigma^2) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\mu)^2\right).\] Apply the key identity from § Gaussian Sampling Model and Sufficient Statistics, \[\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2 + n(\bar x-\mu)^2 = (n-1)s^2 + n(\bar x-\mu)^2,\] using \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2 = (n-1)s^2\) by definition of the unbiased sample variance. Substituting, \[p(D\mid\mu,\sigma^2) = \underbrace{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(n-1)s^2 + n(\bar x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}_{g(\bar x,\,s^2;\,\mu,\sigma^2)}\cdot\underbrace{1}_{h(D)}.\] The data \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) enter only through the pair \((\bar x, s^2)\); the residual factor \(h(D)\equiv 1\) is trivially free of parameters. By the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem, \((\bar x, s^2)\) is jointly sufficient for \((\mu,\sigma^2)\). Equivalently, one could use \((\bar x, S) = (\bar x, (n-1)s^2)\) — they are one-to-one related.
Cross-reference: § Gaussian Sampling Model and Sufficient Statistics (sufficiency definition and the identity \(\sum(x_i-\mu)^2 = S + n(\bar x-\mu)^2\)).


Conjugate Normal–Inverse-Gamma joint posterior. Under prior \((\mu, \sigma^2) \sim \text{NIG}(\mu_0, \kappa_0, \alpha_0, \beta_0)\), write the posterior parameters \((\mu_n, \kappa_n, \alpha_n, \beta_n)\) after observing \(n\) samples with sample mean \(\bar x\) and sum of squares from \(\bar x\) equal to \(S_{xx}\).


Solution. Setup. With prior \((\mu,\sigma^2)\sim\text{NIG}(\mu_0,\kappa_0,\alpha_0,\beta_0)\) — i.e. \(\mu\mid\sigma^2\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\sigma^2/\kappa_0)\) and \(\sigma^2\sim\text{IG}(\alpha_0,\beta_0)\) — and \(n\) Gaussian samples with sample mean \(\bar x\) and centred sum of squares \(S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\), we derive the four posterior hyperparameters. By the NIG posterior parameters in § Joint Inference: Normal-Inverse-Gamma Model, the posterior remains NIG (this is the definition of conjugacy). To derive the updates, write the joint prior as \(p(\mu,\sigma^2)\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(\alpha_0+3/2)}\exp\!\bigl(-[2\beta_0+\kappa_0(\mu-\mu_0)^2]/(2\sigma^2)\bigr)\) and multiply by the likelihood, using the identity \(\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2 = S_{xx} + n(\bar x-\mu)^2\) from § Gaussian Sampling Model and Sufficient Statistics. The exponent becomes \[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\!\Bigl[2\beta_0 + S_{xx} + \kappa_0(\mu-\mu_0)^2 + n(\bar x-\mu)^2\Bigr].\] Completing the square in \(\mu\) from the two quadratic terms: \[\kappa_0(\mu-\mu_0)^2 + n(\mu-\bar x)^2 = (\kappa_0+n)(\mu - \mu_n)^2 + \frac{\kappa_0 n}{\kappa_0+n}(\bar x-\mu_0)^2.\] Reading off coefficients, the posterior parameters are \[\begin{align}
\kappa_n &= \kappa_0 + n, &\mu_n &= \frac{\kappa_0\mu_0 + n\bar x}{\kappa_n},\\
\alpha_n &= \alpha_0 + \tfrac{n}{2}, &\beta_n &= \beta_0 + \tfrac{S_{xx}}{2} + \frac{\kappa_0 n}{2(\kappa_0+n)}(\bar x - \mu_0)^2.
\end{align}\] The exponent in \(\sigma^2\) picks up \(-n/2\) (from the Gaussian factor), giving \(\alpha_n = \alpha_0 + n/2\). The last term of \(\beta_n\) — quadratic in \(\bar x-\mu_0\) — is the extra rate contribution from prior/data disagreement: the more \(\bar x\) differs from \(\mu_0\), the wider the marginal posterior of \(\sigma^2\), because such disagreement is more easily explained by high noise.
Cross-reference: § Joint Inference: Normal-Inverse-Gamma Model (NIG conjugate update definition); § Gaussian Sampling Model and Sufficient Statistics (identity for \(\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\)).


For the NIG conjugate model, derive the marginal posterior \(p(\mu \mid D)\) and identify it as a Student-\(t\) distribution. State its location, scale, and degrees of freedom.


Solution. Setup. From the NIG joint posterior we integrate out \(\sigma^2\) to obtain the marginal for \(\mu\). By the marginal-\(\mu\) Student-\(t\) result in § Joint Inference: Normal-Inverse-Gamma Model, the answer is a shifted-and-scaled Student-\(t\); here we do the integral in detail. The joint posterior kernel is (from the theorem in that section) \[p(\mu,\sigma^2\mid D)\propto (\sigma^2)^{-(\alpha_n+1)}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta_n}{\sigma^2}\right)\cdot (\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\] Collecting the \((\sigma^2)^{-(\alpha_n+3/2)}\) factor and the exponential, we obtain an unnormalised Inverse-Gamma in \(\sigma^2\) with shape \(\alpha_n+1/2\) and rate \[R(\mu) = \beta_n + \frac{\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2}{2}.\] The integral \(\int_0^\infty (\sigma^2)^{-(a+1)}\exp(-R/\sigma^2)\,d\sigma^2 = \Gamma(a)/R^a\) (change of variables \(u=R/\sigma^2\)) yields \[p(\mu\mid D)\propto R(\mu)^{-(\alpha_n+1/2)} = \left[\beta_n\!\left(1 + \frac{\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2}{2\beta_n}\right)\right]^{-(\alpha_n+1/2)} \propto \left[1 + \frac{\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2}{2\beta_n}\right]^{-(\alpha_n+1/2)}.\] Matching to the generalised Student-\(t\) density \([1 + (x-m)^2/(\nu s^2)]^{-(\nu+1)/2}\) we read off \(\nu+1 = 2\alpha_n+1 \Rightarrow \nu = 2\alpha_n\) degrees of freedom, location \(m = \mu_n\), and \(\nu s^2 = 2\beta_n/\kappa_n\) so that the squared scale is \(s^2 = \beta_n/(\alpha_n\kappa_n)\). Therefore \[\mu\mid D \sim t_{2\alpha_n}\!\left(\mu_n,\ \frac{\beta_n}{\alpha_n\kappa_n}\right).\] The heavy \(t\) tails encode the extra uncertainty from marginalising over \(\sigma^2\); as \(\alpha_n\to\infty\) (large \(n\)), \(t_{2\alpha_n} \to \mathcal{N}\).
Cross-reference: § Joint Inference: Normal-Inverse-Gamma Model (marginal-\(\mu\) theorem, and the joint NIG kernel formula just before it).


Posterior predictive in the conjugate Normal model with known \(\sigma^2\). Derive \(p(x_{\text{new}} \mid D)\) when \(\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)\) and the data have sample mean \(\bar x\).


Solution. Setup. With known \(\sigma^2\) and posterior \(\mu\mid D \sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_n,V_n)\) from the Normal–Normal conjugate model, derive the posterior predictive density for a fresh observation \(x_{\text{new}}\). By the Normal–Normal conjugate update (§ Inference of the Mean with Known Variance), the posterior parameters are \(\mu_n = (\mu_0/\sigma_0^2 + n\bar x/\sigma^2)/\kappa_n\) and \(V_n = \kappa_n^{-1} = 1/(1/\sigma_0^2 + n/\sigma^2)\). The posterior predictive is defined (§ Posterior Predictive Distribution) as \[p(x_{\text{new}}\mid D) = \int p(x_{\text{new}}\mid\mu,\sigma^2)\,p(\mu\mid D)\,d\mu.\] Substitute the two Gaussians: \[p(x_{\text{new}}\mid D) \propto \int\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_{\text{new}}-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}-\frac{(\mu-\mu_n)^2}{2V_n}\right)d\mu.\] The exponent is quadratic in \(\mu\); completing the square in \(\mu\) collects \(\mu^2(1/\sigma^2 + 1/V_n)/2\) and a linear part, leaving a residual quadratic in \(x_{\text{new}}\) independent of \(\mu\). Performing the Gaussian integral in \(\mu\) leaves that residual, which — after simplification using \(1/(1/\sigma^2 + 1/V_n) = \sigma^2 V_n/(\sigma^2+V_n)\) — reduces to \(-\tfrac{1}{2}(x_{\text{new}}-\mu_n)^2/(\sigma^2+V_n)\). Equivalently, writing \(x_{\text{new}} = \mu + \epsilon\) with \(\mu\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_n,V_n)\) and \(\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\) independent, the sum of independent Gaussians is Gaussian with mean \(\mu_n\) and variance \(V_n+\sigma^2\). Therefore \[x_{\text{new}}\mid D \sim \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\mu_n,\ V_n + \sigma^2\bigr).\] The mean equals the posterior mean of \(\mu\); the predictive variance decomposes into parameter uncertainty \(V_n\) plus irreducible sampling noise \(\sigma^2\).
Cross-reference: § Posterior Predictive Distribution (definition); § Inference of the Mean with Known Variance (posterior form \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_n,V_n)\)).


For the conjugate model with known \(\sigma^2\), derive the \(95\%\) equal-tailed credible interval for \(\mu\) using the conjugate posterior parameters \((\mu_n, V_n)\). Use \(z_{0.975} \approx 2\).


Solution. Setup. With known variance, derive the equal-tailed \(95\%\) credible interval for \(\mu\) using the posterior parameters \((\mu_n,V_n)\). By the Normal–Normal conjugate update (§ Inference of the Mean with Known Variance), the posterior is \(\mu\mid D \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n, V_n)\) with \(V_n = \kappa_n^{-1}\). A central (equal-tailed) \((1-\alpha)\) credible interval \([a,b]\) satisfies \(P(\mu<a\mid D) = P(\mu>b\mid D) = \alpha/2\). Standardise: let \(Z = (\mu-\mu_n)/\sqrt{V_n}\), which under the posterior is \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). The equal-tailed condition becomes \(P(Z < -z_{1-\alpha/2}) = P(Z > z_{1-\alpha/2}) = \alpha/2\), where \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) is the standard-normal \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile. Un-standardising gives \[\bigl[\,\mu_n - z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{V_n},\ \ \mu_n + z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{V_n}\,\bigr].\] For \(\alpha = 0.05\), \(z_{0.975} \approx 1.96 \approx 2\), so the \(95\%\) credible interval is \[\boxed{\ \mu_n \pm 2\sqrt{V_n}.\ }\] This is the same functional form as the § Credible Intervals and Regions central-interval formula, with the Student-\(t\) quantile replaced by the normal quantile because \(\sigma^2\) is known (no marginalisation needed). In the large-\(n\) limit of the NIG model the \(t\)-interval reduces to this one — see § Credible Intervals and Regions.
Cross-reference: § Inference of the Mean with Known Variance (posterior \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_n,V_n)\)); § Credible Intervals and Regions (central credible interval formula).


Sequential updating. With known \(\sigma^2\) and prior \(\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)\), you observe data in two batches with sample means \(\bar x_1, \bar x_2\) and counts \(n_1, n_2\). Show that updating sequentially gives the same posterior as updating in one batch.


Solution. After batch 1: \(\kappa_1 = 1/\tau^2 + n_1/\sigma^2\) and \(\mu_1 = \kappa_1^{-1}(n_1\bar x_1/\sigma^2)\). Using this as prior for batch 2: \[\kappa_n = \kappa_1 + n_2/\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n_1+n_2}{\sigma^2},\qquad \mu_n = \kappa_n^{-1}\!\left(\kappa_1\mu_1 + \frac{n_2\bar x_2}{\sigma^2}\right) = \kappa_n^{-1}\!\left(\frac{n_1\bar x_1 + n_2\bar x_2}{\sigma^2}\right),\] which is identical to the one-shot update with pooled mean \((n_1\bar x_1 + n_2\bar x_2)/(n_1+n_2)\) and count \(n_1+n_2\). Precisions and precision-weighted means simply concatenate.


Posterior predictive variance decomposition. Show that the posterior predictive variance in the conjugate Normal model is \(V_n + \sigma^2\), and identify which term is parameter uncertainty and which is irreducible noise.


Solution. By the law of total variance, \[\mathrm{Var}(x_{\text{new}}\mid D) = \mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathrm{Var}(x_{\text{new}}\mid\mu)] + \mathrm{Var}_\mu[\mathbb{E}(x_{\text{new}}\mid\mu)] = \sigma^2 + V_n.\] Here \(\sigma^2\) is the irreducible observation noise and \(V_n = \kappa_n^{-1}\) is the posterior (parameter) uncertainty about \(\mu\).


Multivariate conjugate update. For \(\mathbf x \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\) with \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) known and prior \(\boldsymbol\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu_0, \boldsymbol\Sigma_0)\), write the posterior \(p(\boldsymbol\mu \mid D)\) after observing one sample \(\mathbf x\).


Solution. Precision matrices add and the posterior mean is precision-weighted: \[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1},\qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_n = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n\!\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_0^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0 + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf x\right),\] so \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\mid D \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n)\).


Bayesian \(z\)-test. With prior \(\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)\) and known \(\sigma^2\), compute the Bayes factor between \(H_0:\mu = 0\) and \(H_1:\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)\) as a function of the standardised sample mean \(z = \bar x \sqrt{n}/\sigma\). (You can reuse the worked example “Closed-form Bayes factor for a Gaussian mean” in Chapter 4.)


Solution. Let \(g = n\tau^2/\sigma^2\) measure prior relative to data precision. The marginal likelihood under \(H_1\) inflates the data variance by the prior, while \(H_0\) uses just \(\sigma^2/n\). Standard Gaussian marginalisation (Ch. 4) gives \[\mathrm{BF}_{10} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+g}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{g}{1+g}\cdot\frac{z^2}{2}\right).\] Large \(|z|\) exponentially favours \(H_1\); the prefactor \((1+g)^{-1/2}\) is the Ockham penalty for the broader alternative.


Improper Jeffreys prior for the variance. Take \(p(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2\). Show that the posterior for \(\sigma^2\) given \(n\) i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) samples is Inverse-Gamma, and identify its parameters.


Solution. The Jeffreys prior is the formal limit \(\alpha_0 \to 0,\ \beta_0 \to 0\) of \(\text{IG}(\alpha_0,\beta_0)\). Multiplying by the likelihood \(\propto (\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp(-S/(2\sigma^2))\) with \(S = \sum_i x_i^2\) gives \[\sigma^2 \mid D \sim \text{IG}\!\left(\alpha_n = \tfrac{n}{2},\ \beta_n = \tfrac{S}{2}\right),\] which is proper for \(n \ge 1\).


Posterior comparison. With \(n = 9\), \(\sigma^2 = 4\), \(\bar x = 3\): compute the posterior mean for \(\mu\) under the flat prior, the \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) prior, and the \(\mathcal{N}(0, 100)\) prior. Comment on how the posterior depends on prior width.


Solution. Data precision is \(n/\sigma^2 = 9/4 = 2.25\). The precision-weighted-mean form \(\mu_n = (n\bar x/\sigma^2)/(1/\sigma_0^2 + n/\sigma^2)\) gives \[\mu_n^{\text{flat}} = \bar x = 3,\qquad \mu_n^{(\sigma_0^2 = 1)} = \frac{27/4}{1 + 9/4} = \frac{27}{13} \approx 2.08,\qquad \mu_n^{(\sigma_0^2 = 100)} = \frac{27/4}{0.01 + 9/4} \approx 2.99.\] A tight prior (\(\sigma_0^2 = 1\)) shrinks the estimate sharply toward \(\mu_0 = 0\); a vague prior (\(\sigma_0^2 = 100\)) recovers the flat-prior MLE to within \(1\%\). Posterior dependence on prior width vanishes as \(\sigma_0^2 \to \infty\).


Sample size and prior dominance. For the conjugate Normal–Normal model with prior precision \(\tau_0\) and likelihood precision \(n/\sigma^2\), find the sample size \(n^\star\) such that the posterior is half-determined by the prior and half by the data.


Solution. Equal weighting means prior precision equals data precision: \(\tau_0 = n^\star/\sigma^2\), so \[n^\star = \tau_0\,\sigma^2.\] For \(n \ll n^\star\) the prior dominates, while for \(n \gg n^\star\) the likelihood dominates and the posterior approaches the flat-prior result.

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.1 Motivation and the curse of dimensionality
In Bayesian inference, the central computational challenge is to evaluate expectations of the form \[\mathbb{E}_\pi[f(\theta)] = \int f(\theta) \pi(\theta \mid D) \, d\theta,\] where \(\pi(\theta \mid D)\) is the posterior distribution. These integrals appear everywhere: computing the evidence, credible intervals, point estimates, and predictions. Most realistic models lack analytical solutions, especially in high dimensions.
Classical numerical integration methods fail catastrophically in high dimensions. Consider a grid-based quadrature with \(n\) points per dimension in a \(d\)-dimensional space. The total number of grid points grows as \(N = n^d\)—exponential in dimension. This is the curse of dimensionality for deterministic methods.
Monte Carlo to the rescue. Monte Carlo methods replace high-dimensional integration with averaging over random samples. The fundamental principle is
\[\mathbb{E}_p[f(X)] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i), \quad x_i \sim p(x).\]
By the law of large numbers, this average converges to the true expectation as \(N \to \infty\). Crucially, the error does not depend explicitly on dimension.
However, there is a catch: while the error rate is independent of dimension, the variance \(\text{Var}_p(f)\) itself can grow exponentially with \(d\). For the hypercube example, the variance approaches zero as \(d \to \infty\) (since \(I_d \to 0\)), but the relative error \[\frac{\sqrt{\text{Var}(\widehat{I}_N)}}{\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I}_N]} \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{N I_d}} \to \infty\] explodes exponentially. We need \(N \sim 1/I_d\) to maintain constant relative error—which is infeasible for rare events. Techniques like rejection sampling and importance sampling exist precisely to mitigate this degeneracy by concentrating samples where the integrand is large.
Show code
# True integral: volume of ball of radius 0.5 in [0,1]^d
true_val <- function(d) {
  pi^(d/2) / gamma(d/2 + 1) * 2^(-2*d)
}

# Naive MC
dims <- c(2, 5, 10, 15, 20)
N <- 1e6
results <- data.frame(d = dims, est = NA, rel_err = NA)

for (i in seq_along(dims)) {
  d <- dims[i]
  x <- matrix(runif(N * d), ncol = d)
  inside <- rowSums(x^2) < 0.25
  est <- mean(inside)
  true <- true_val(d)
  rel_err <- if (true > 0) abs(est - true) / true else NA
  results$est[i] <- est
  results$rel_err[i] <- rel_err
}

# Plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1))

plot(results$d, results$est, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 1.2, lwd = 2,
     col = rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.8), log = "y",
     xlab = "Dimension d", ylab = "Estimated I_d",
     main = "Hypersphere volume (log scale)", ylim = c(1e-15, 1))


Warning in xy.coords(x, y, xlabel, ylabel, log): 2 y values <= 0 omitted from
logarithmic plot


Show code
lines(results$d, true_val(results$d), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("MC estimate", "True value"),
       col = c(rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.8), "red"), lwd = 2, pch = c(16, NA))

plot(results$d, results$rel_err, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 1.2, lwd = 2,
     col = rgb(0.8, 0.2, 0.2), log = "y",
     xlab = "Dimension d", ylab = "Relative error",
     main = "Relative error (log scale)")





Naive uniform sampling in high-dimensional hypersphere: both relative and absolute error grow exponentially with dimension.

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
Consider the integral over a unit hypercube \([0,1]^d\) with an indicator function that counts volume inside a ball of radius \(r = 1/2\) centered at the origin: \[I_d = \int_{[0,1]^d} \mathbb{1}_{\|x\| < 1/2} \, dx.\]
The volume of the region is proportional to \(r^d\) while the hypercube has volume 1. As \(d\) grows, nearly all of the hypercube’s volume lies outside the ball (since \(V_{\text{ball}} / V_{\text{cube}} \sim (1/2)^d \to 0\)). A uniform grid wastes almost all points. Even with \(N = 10^6\) samples in dimension \(d = 20\), we expect essentially zero hits, making the variance unbounded and estimation impossible.





Let \(x_1, \ldots, x_N \sim p(x)\) be i.i.d. samples. The Monte Carlo estimator \[\widehat{I}_N = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i)\] satisfies: - Unbiasedness: \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I}_N] = \mathbb{E}_p[f(X)]\) - Variance: \(\text{Var}(\widehat{I}_N) = \frac{1}{N} \text{Var}_p(f)\) - Convergence: \(\widehat{I}_N - \mathbb{E}_p[f] = \mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})\)
The error scales universally as \(N^{-1/2}\) regardless of dimension \(d\).




Explain why Monte Carlo methods are central in Bayesian inference. What is the difference between using independent posterior samples and samples generated by a Markov chain?
Solution. Bayesian inference is built on posterior expectations, \[E[f(\theta) \mid D] = \int f(\theta)\,p(\theta \mid D)\,d\theta.\] In moderate to high dimensions, deterministic grid integration becomes impractical because the number of grid points grows exponentially with the parameter dimension (curse of dimensionality). Monte Carlo replaces the integral by an average over samples: \[E[f(\theta) \mid D] \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(\theta_i), \qquad \theta_i \sim p(\theta \mid D).\] If the samples \(\theta_i\) are independent, the variance of the estimator scales as \(\text{Var}(f)/N\). With MCMC the samples are correlated by construction, so the variance is inflated by the integrated autocorrelation time \(\tau_{\text{int}}\): \[\text{Var}(\widehat I_N) \approx \frac{\tau_{\text{int}}}{N}\,\text{Var}_\pi(f).\] The relevant sample size is therefore the effective sample size \(N_{\text{eff}} \approx N/\tau_{\text{int}}\), not the raw chain length. MCMC remains valid after burn-in and convergence to the stationary distribution, but reporting \(N_{\text{eff}}\) — not \(N\) — is essential.

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.2 Direct sampling: inverse transform method
The most straightforward sampling approach is the inverse transform method (or inverse CDF method). It is exact and works whenever the CDF can be computed and inverted analytically.

Let \(F(x) = P(X \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^x p(x') \, dx'\) be the cumulative distribution function of a continuous random variable \(X \sim p(x)\). The inverse transform method generates samples by: 1. Compute \(F(x)\) and its inverse \(F^{-1}(u)\) (the quantile function). 2. Sample \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). 3. Set \(X = F^{-1}(U)\).
Then \(X \sim p(x)\).

Proof: By the probability integral transform, \[P(X \le x) = P(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = P(U \le F(x)) = F(x),\] so the distribution of \(X\) is \(p(x)\) as required.
Example: exponential distribution. For \(p(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) with \(x \ge 0\), the CDF is \(F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}\). Inverting \(u = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}\) gives \[x = -\frac{1}{\lambda} \log(1-u).\] Since \(1 - U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) when \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\), we have \[X = -\frac{1}{\lambda} \log(U).\]


Show code
N <- 10000
u <- runif(N)
lambda <- 2
x <- -log(u) / lambda
x_builtin <- rexp(N, rate = lambda)

hist(x, probability = TRUE, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.4),
     breaks = 50, main = "Inverse transform vs. rexp",
     xlab = "x", xlim = c(0, 3))
hist(x_builtin, probability = TRUE, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.4),
     breaks = 50, add = TRUE)
curve(dexp(x, rate = lambda), col = "darkred", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
legend("topright", legend = c("Inverse transform", "rexp"),
       fill = c(rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.4), rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.4)))





Overlaid histograms show agreement between inverse-transform (red) and built-in (blue) exponential samples.




The inverse transform method is exact, simple, and efficient in one dimension. However, it requires analytical inversion of \(F\), which is rarely available for complex distributions (e.g., posteriors) or in high dimensions.

Let \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) and define \(X = -\lambda^{-1}\log(1 - U)\) with \(\lambda > 0\). Find the density of \(X\) and explain the Monte Carlo interpretation.
Solution. For \(x \geq 0\), \[P(X \leq x) = P\!\left(-\lambda^{-1}\log(1 - U) \leq x\right) = P\!\left(U \leq 1 - e^{-\lambda x}\right) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}.\] Differentiating gives \(f_X(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x \geq 0\). Thus the inverse-CDF construction transforms uniform random numbers into exponential waiting times with rate \(\lambda\). This is the simplest non-trivial Monte Carlo recipe and underlies almost every random-number generator in Poisson process simulation.

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.3 Rejection sampling
When the target density \(\pi(x)\) is difficult to sample from directly, rejection sampling uses a proposal distribution \(q(x)\) from which sampling is easy, and accepts or rejects each proposal to asymptotically recover the target.

Suppose we want to sample from a target \(\pi(x) = \tilde{\pi}(x) / Z\) where \(\tilde{\pi}(x)\) is the unnormalized density and \(Z\) is unknown. Choose a proposal density \(q(x)\) with the same support. If there exists \(M > 0\) such that \[\tilde{\pi}(x) \le M \, q(x) \quad \forall x,\] then the following algorithm produces samples from \(\pi(x)\):
Rejection Sampling Algorithm: 1. Sample \(x \sim q(x)\). 2. Sample \(u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). 3. Accept \(x\) if \(u \le \tilde{\pi}(x) / (M q(x))\); else reject and repeat.
The accepted samples are i.i.d. from \(\pi(x)\).

Correctness: The joint density of proposing and accepting is \[p(x, \text{accept}) = q(x) \cdot \frac{\tilde{\pi}(x)}{M q(x)} = \frac{\tilde{\pi}(x)}{M}.\] The marginal acceptance probability is \[P(\text{accept}) = \int \frac{\tilde{\pi}(x)}{M} \, dx = \frac{Z}{M},\] and conditioning on acceptance yields \[p(x \mid \text{accept}) = \frac{\tilde{\pi}(x)/M}{Z/M} = \frac{\tilde{\pi}(x)}{Z} = \pi(x).\]
Acceptance ratio and efficiency. The acceptance probability is \(P(\text{accept}) = Z / M\). For efficiency, we want \(M\) as small as possible (ideally \(M^* = \max_x [\tilde{\pi}(x) / q(x)]\)). When acceptance probability is low, most computational effort is wasted on rejected proposals.
In high dimensions, rejection sampling becomes pathologically inefficient. Consider sampling from a Gaussian target in dimension \(d\). A reasonably-scaled proposal will have acceptance probability that typically decays as \(e^{-\alpha d}\) for some constant \(\alpha > 0\). The algorithm wastes an exponentially growing fraction of samples, making it impractical for large \(d\).

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.4 Importance sampling
Importance sampling avoids the rejection step by using weighted samples. Every sample is retained, but weighted by how much the proposal underestimates the target.

To compute \(\mathbb{E}_\pi[f(\theta)] = \int f(\theta) \pi(\theta) \, d\theta\), rewrite the integral in terms of a proposal \(q(\theta)\) with the same support: \[\mathbb{E}_\pi[f] = \int f(\theta) \pi(\theta) \, d\theta = \int f(\theta) \frac{\pi(\theta)}{q(\theta)} q(\theta) \, d\theta = \mathbb{E}_q\left[ f(\theta) w(\theta) \right],\] where the importance weight is \[w(\theta) = \frac{\pi(\theta)}{q(\theta)}.\]
Sample \(\theta_i \sim q(\theta)\) i.i.d. and estimate \[\widehat{I} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(\theta_i) w(\theta_i).\] This is unbiased when \(\pi\) is known up to a normalizing constant.

Self-normalized importance sampling. In practice, the target \(\pi(\theta)\) is often known only up to normalization: \(\pi(\theta) = \tilde{\pi}(\theta) / Z\) where \(Z\) is unknown (as in Bayesian posteriors). Use unnormalized weights \(\tilde{w}_i = \tilde{\pi}(\theta_i) / q(\theta_i)\) and estimate via the ratio \[\widehat{I} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N f(\theta_i) \tilde{w}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{w}_i}.\] This estimator is biased but consistent (converges to the true value as \(N \to \infty\)).
The efficiency of importance sampling depends critically on how well the weights match the target distribution. If the proposal \(q\) is far from the target \(\pi\), most weight concentrates on a few samples, and the effective sample size collapses.

The effective sample size (ESS) quantifies this degeneracy: \[\text{ESS} = \frac{(\sum_i \tilde{w}_i)^2}{\sum_i \tilde{w}_i^2}.\]
Intuitively, if all weights are equal (\(\tilde{w}_i = \tilde{w}^*\)), then \(\text{ESS} = N\). If one weight dominates, \(\text{ESS} \ll N\), signaling weight degeneracy. As a rule of thumb, \(\text{ESS} < N / 10\) indicates serious efficiency loss.

Optimal proposal. The variance of the importance-sampling estimator is proportional to \(\mathbb{E}_q[(f(X) w(X))^2]\). By calculus of variations, the variance-minimizing proposal is \[q^*(x) \propto |f(x)| \pi(x).\] However, this optimal proposal is itself as difficult to sample from as \(\pi\), so it is rarely useful in practice. Practical guidance: match the shape and tail behavior of \(\pi\), ensure heavy tails to avoid undersampling the tail regions, and capture correlations.
High-dimensional limitations. In very high dimensions, any suboptimal proposal leads to catastrophic weight degeneracy. The mass of \(\pi\) concentrates in thin, high-curvature regions (e.g., the typical set of a high-dimensional Gaussian). Unless \(q\) places comparable mass in those regions, the ESS shrinks exponentially with dimension. This is a fundamental curse of dimensionality for importance sampling, which motivates the turn to Markov chain methods.

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.5 Variance reduction
Before moving to MCMC, two classical variance-reduction tricks deserve mention.

Antithetic sampling: Use correlated pairs to reduce variance. If \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\), sample both \(U\) and \(1-U\) (which is also uniform). Since \(f(F^{-1}(U))\) and \(f(F^{-1}(1-U))\) are negatively correlated for many smooth functions, averaging them reduces variance.
Control variates: If you know the expectation of a related function \(g(x)\) under \(\pi\), use \[\widehat{I}_{\text{cv}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i [f(x_i) - c(g(x_i) - \mathbb{E}[g])]\] for a suitably chosen \(c\). The term \(c(g(x_i) - \mathbb{E}[g])\) has zero mean but can have large negative correlation with \(f(x_i) - \mathbb{E}[f]\), reducing variance.

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.6 Markov chains and stationarity
When neither inverse sampling, rejection, nor importance sampling are practical, we turn to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The key idea is to construct a stochastic dynamics whose long-time distribution equals the target \(\pi(x)\).

A Markov chain is a discrete-time stochastic process \(\{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}\) where the next state depends only on the current state (the Markov property): \[P(X_{t+1} = x' \mid X_t = x, X_{t-1}, \ldots, X_0) = P(X_{t+1} = x' \mid X_t = x) \equiv T(x \to x').\]
The transition operator \(T(x \to x')\) is the core object; it specifies how the chain evolves in a single step.

Stationarity: A distribution \(\pi(x)\) is stationary with respect to \(T\) if \[\pi(x) = \sum_{x'} T(x' \to x) \pi(x'),\] or in integral form, \[\pi(x) = \int T(x' \to x) \pi(x') \, dx'.\] Under one transition step, the distribution remains unchanged.
Convergence: For the chain to be useful, we need it to converge to \(\pi\) starting from any initial distribution \(p_0\). This requires: - Irreducibility: all states (or regions) are mutually reachable with positive probability. - Aperiodicity: the chain does not cycle with a fixed period.
Under these conditions, the distribution evolves as \[p_t(x) = T^t p_0(x) \xrightarrow{t \to \infty} \pi(x).\]

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.7 Detailed balance and reversibility
A sufficient condition for stationarity is detailed balance: \[\pi(x) T(x \to x') = \pi(x') T(x' \to x) \quad \forall x, x'.\]
This says that the probability current from \(x\) to \(x'\) balances the current from \(x'\) to \(x\) at equilibrium. While not necessary for stationarity (some stationary distributions have non-zero net currents), detailed balance is mathematically convenient and physically intuitive—it ensures the chain is reversible.

A Markov chain on states \(\{0, 1\}\) has transition probabilities \(P(0 \to 1) = a\) and \(P(1 \to 0) = b\), with \(a, b \in (0, 1)\). Find the stationary distribution and verify detailed balance.
Solution. Let the stationary distribution be \((\pi_0, \pi_1)\). Stationarity requires the probability flow out of \(0\) to equal the flow in: \[\pi_0\,a = \pi_1\,b, \qquad \pi_0 + \pi_1 = 1.\] Solving, \[\pi_0 = \frac{b}{a + b}, \qquad \pi_1 = \frac{a}{a + b}.\] Detailed balance asks \(\pi_0\,P(0 \to 1) = \pi_1\,P(1 \to 0)\). Substituting, \[\frac{b}{a + b}\,a = \frac{a}{a + b}\,b,\] which holds trivially. In two-state chains stationarity and detailed balance are equivalent — any stationary distribution is automatically reversible.

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.8 Metropolis–Hastings algorithm
The Metropolis–Hastings (MH) algorithm constructs a transition operator satisfying detailed balance by combining a proposal \(q(x' \mid x)\) with an accept/reject step.

Given a target \(\pi(x)\) (known up to normalization), the MH transition is \[T(x \to x') = q(x' \mid x) \, \alpha(x \to x'),\] where the acceptance probability is \[\alpha(x \to x') = \min\left(1, \frac{\pi(x') q(x \mid x')}{\pi(x) q(x' \mid x)}\right).\]
This is the MH ratio or Hastings ratio.

Proof of detailed balance: Define the ratio \(r(x, x') = \frac{\pi(x') q(x \mid x')}{\pi(x) q(x' \mid x)}\).
Case 1: \(r \ge 1\). Then \(\alpha(x \to x') = 1\) and \(\alpha(x' \to x) = 1/r\), so \[\pi(x) q(x' \mid x) \alpha(x \to x') = \pi(x) q(x' \mid x) = \pi(x') q(x \mid x') \cdot \frac{1}{r} = \pi(x') q(x \mid x') \alpha(x' \to x).\]
Case 2: \(r < 1\). Then \(\alpha(x \to x') = r\) and \(\alpha(x' \to x) = 1\), giving the same identity.
Thus detailed balance holds, and \(\pi\) is stationary. \(\square\)
Practical MH algorithm. One step from the current state \(x_t\):

Propose \(x' \sim q(x' \mid x_t)\).
Compute the ratio \(r = \pi(x') q(x_t \mid x') / [\pi(x_t) q(x' \mid x_t)]\).
Draw \(u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\).
Accept if \(u < \min(1, r)\) and set \(x_{t+1} = x'\); reject otherwise and set \(x_{t+1} = x_t\).

For a symmetric proposal \(q(x' \mid x) = q(x \mid x')\) (e.g., a Gaussian random walk), the acceptance probability simplifies to \[\alpha(x \to x') = \min\left(1, \frac{\pi(x')}{\pi(x)}\right).\]

title: 8  Monte Carlo methods
text:
8.9 Convergence and ergodicity
After an initial burn-in period during which the chain forgets its starting point, the samples \(x_t\) are approximately distributed as \(\pi(x)\). Estimates are formed as time averages: \[\widehat{I} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^N f(x_t) \approx \mathbb{E}_\pi[f].\]
However, successive samples are correlated. The integrated autocorrelation time \[\tau_{\text{int}} = 1 + 2 \sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_f(k)\] quantifies this correlation, where \(\rho_f(k)\) is the normalized autocorrelation at lag \(k\). The effective number of independent samples is \[N_{\text{eff}} \approx \frac{N}{2 \tau_{\text{int}}},\] which can be much smaller than the total number of draws.
The decay of autocorrelation is controlled by the spectral gap of the transition operator—the inverse of the largest non-zero eigenvalue. A small gap indicates slow mixing and long memory, forcing either longer chains or better proposals.

A single MCMC chain has \(N = 20\,000\) stored samples. The estimated normalised autocorrelation is approximately \(\rho(\tau) = 0.8^\tau\) for \(\tau \geq 1\). Estimate \(\tau_{\text{int}}\) and \(N_{\text{eff}}\) using \[\tau_{\text{int}} = 1 + 2\sum_{\tau=1}^\infty \rho(\tau).\]
Solution. The tail is a geometric series: \[\sum_{\tau=1}^\infty 0.8^\tau = \frac{0.8}{1 - 0.8} = 4.\] Hence \[\tau_{\text{int}} = 1 + 2\cdot 4 = 9, \qquad N_{\text{eff}} \approx \frac{N}{\tau_{\text{int}}} = \frac{20\,000}{9} \approx 2\,222.\] The chain contains far less information than its raw length suggests — long-memory autocorrelation discounts every additional sample.


For a stationary Markov chain \(\{x_t\}_{t=1}^N\) and an observable \(A(x)\), define the autocorrelation function, the normalised autocorrelation function, and the integrated autocorrelation time. If \(M = 5\) independent chains each have length \(N = 10^4\) and the integrated autocorrelation time is \(\tau_{\text{int}} = 250\), estimate the total effective sample size. Is it acceptable or should the proposal be improved?
Solution. The autocorrelation function of \(A\) is \[C_A(\tau) = E[A(x_t)\,A(x_{t+\tau})] - E[A]^2,\] the normalised version is \(\rho_A(\tau) = C_A(\tau)/C_A(0)\), and \[\tau_{\text{int}} = 1 + 2\sum_{\tau=1}^\infty \rho_A(\tau).\] With \(M = 5\) chains of length \(N = 10^4\), the total number of stored samples is \(N_{\text{tot}} = M N = 5\cdot 10^4\). Inflating the variance by \(\tau_{\text{int}}\), \[N_{\text{eff}} \approx \frac{N_{\text{tot}}}{\tau_{\text{int}}} = \frac{5\cdot 10^4}{250} = 200.\] Five correlated chains carry the same information as roughly \(2\cdot 10^2\) independent draws. The ratio \(N/\tau_{\text{int}} = 40\) per chain shows that most moves are wasteful — the proposal is poorly matched to the target geometry, and either a better proposal (HMC, adapted scale) or a reparametrisation is needed.



Show code
# Target: mixture of two Gaussians
target_density <- function(x) {
  0.5 * dnorm(x, mean = -3, sd = 1) + 0.5 * dnorm(x, mean = 3, sd = 1)
}

log_target <- function(x) log(target_density(x))

# MH sampler
mh_sample <- function(n_steps, x0, proposal_sd) {
  x <- numeric(n_steps)
  x[1] <- x0
  n_accept <- 0
  for (t in 2:n_steps) {
    x_current <- x[t - 1]
    x_prop <- rnorm(1, mean = x_current, sd = proposal_sd)
    log_r <- log_target(x_prop) - log_target(x_current)
    if (log(runif(1)) < log_r) {
      x[t] <- x_prop
      n_accept <- n_accept + 1
    } else {
      x[t] <- x_current
    }
  }
  list(samples = x, accept_rate = n_accept / (n_steps - 1))
}

# Run sampler
n_steps <- 50000
burn_in <- 5000
proposal_sd <- 2.0
mh <- mh_sample(n_steps, x0 = -8, proposal_sd = proposal_sd)
samples <- mh$samples
samples_burn <- samples[(burn_in + 1):n_steps]

cat("Acceptance rate:", mh$accept_rate, "\n")


Acceptance rate: 0.5310906


Show code
# Compute autocorrelation
lag_max <- 500
acf_vals <- acf(samples_burn, lag.max = lag_max, plot = FALSE)
lags <- as.numeric(acf_vals$lag)
rho <- as.numeric(acf_vals$acf)

# Integrated autocorrelation time
t_int <- 1 + 2 * sum(rho[2:min(which(abs(rho[-1]) < 0.05)[1], length(rho))])
N_eff <- length(samples_burn) / (2 * t_int)

cat("Integrated autocorr time:", round(t_int, 2), "\n")


Integrated autocorr time: 42.19


Show code
cat("N_eff:", round(N_eff, 0), "\n")


N_eff: 533


Show code
# Plots
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

# Trace before and after burn-in
plot(1:burn_in, samples[1:burn_in], type = "l", xlab = "Iteration",
     ylab = "x", main = "Before burn-in", lwd = 0.5, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.6))

plot((burn_in + 1):n_steps, samples_burn, type = "l",
     xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "x", main = "After burn-in",
     lwd = 0.5, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.6))

# Histogram + target
hist(samples_burn, breaks = 80, probability = TRUE,
     main = "Posterior samples", xlab = "x",
     col = rgb(0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 0.4), border = NA)
curve(target_density(x), from = -8, to = 8, lwd = 2, col = "red", add = TRUE)





Trace plot of chain (before and after burn-in), histogram, and autocorrelation. Low acceptance rate (ca. 47%) due to small proposal variance.
